name: Felix Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sports reporter for the regional daily's website, covering the two lower-league football clubs and the rugby side. Saturdays I'm in a cold press box running a live blog, then writing the match report on my laptop before the floodlights go off. Weekdays it's training ground interviews, injury news, transfer rumours and a lot of chasing the clubs' press officers. I love match days; what grinds me down is the click targets and writing the same 'five things we learned' piece every week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio flat near the station, which eats most of my pay. I play five-a-side on Wednesdays and that's about my only luxury. I've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank, and my car insurance renewal is coming up in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's fine for the boring stuff like turning the league table into a graphic, and that's about it. I've used it to tidy up quotes once or twice. Nobody's going to read a machine's take on a derby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but not relaxed. The website still lives and dies on clicks, and the owners keep merging sports desks across the group. I'm one of two sports reporters for the whole region now, and that used to be five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, and use the tools now and then for stats and quote tidying. I'd shop around hard on the car insurance and maybe drop the five-a-side for a couple of months. I'd also try to get a few freelance shifts doing radio commentary for the local station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Nothing's on fire, but it's never exactly comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the other three sports reporters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two took redundancy and one went to work for a betting company writing previews, which pays twice as much. I think about that sometimes. I don't really want to write for gambling firms though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the radio shifts bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty or seventy quid a match, a few times a month in the season. It's not much, but it's the difference between paying the insurance in one go or on the card. And I like doing it.

say: AI is fine for **boring stuff** like league table graphics, and that's about it.
Nobody's going to read **a machine's take** on a derby.
think: He'd be **relieved** but not relaxed, since the site still lives on clicks.
Sports desks keep **merging**: he's one of two sports reporters left from five.
do: Keep using tools **now and then** for stats and tidying quotes.
Shop around on the **car insurance** and pause five-a-side for a while.
Pick up **radio commentary** shifts for about sixty or seventy a match.
feel: **Uneasy**: nothing's on fire, but it's never comfortable.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to read a machine's take on a derby.
fieldNote: His own job looks **safe for now**, but desk mergers keep it on his mind.
Tempted but uneasy about **betting firms**, which pay double.
Looks for **small extra income** before cutting deeper.

steps.text: Keep covering the two football clubs and the rugby side
Shop around for cheaper car insurance before January
Pick up paid radio commentary shifts on match days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say match reports are going to be written by machines and readers should demand to know which ones. I'd also say the bit that matters is being at the ground, talking to the manager after a bad defeat. I'd be fairly balanced about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the written side of my job is in real trouble. A machine can take the live data feed and write a decent match report in seconds, and the website would love that. I think they'd keep me for interviews and the odd feature, maybe on fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw a couple of other sites doing it, I'd learn the tools so I can be the person who checks and improves the machine's copy fast. I'd push more into video, filming short interviews on my phone at the training ground, because that's harder to fake. I'd also apply for media officer jobs at the clubs themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see moves to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A club media officer job, wouldn't that mean writing what the club wants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, basically, it's the other side of the fence. I've thought about it. But it's steady money and I'd still be at every game, and plenty of good journalists have done it for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours were cut, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe, because the grounds are on bus routes. Then the five-a-side. I'd keep the phone and the broadband no matter what, because I need them for work.

say: **Match reports** will be machine-written, and readers should know which ones.
What matters is **being at the ground**, talking to the manager after a bad defeat.
think: The **written side** of his job is in real trouble, since data feeds can write reports.
He expects to be kept for interviews and features, maybe on **fewer hours**.
do: Learn the tools once **other sites** prove them, to check machine copy fast.
Film short **video interviews** on his phone at the training ground.
Apply for **club media officer** jobs at the local clubs.
feel: **Anxious**, but he can see moves to make.
S1.quote: A machine can take the live data feed and write a decent match report in seconds, and the website would love that.
fieldNote: Clear-eyed that **match reports** are among the first things to automate.
His **steady** style shows: he waits for proof, then moves quickly.
Willing to cross to **club media**, accepting the loss of independence.

steps.text: Learn to check and fix AI match reports quickly
Film short phone interviews at the training ground each week
Apply for media officer jobs at the two local clubs
Sell the car and switch to buses to grounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is happening too fast and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. I'd say it calmly, but I'd mean it. I'd share stuff online from people who know more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 my job as a reporter is gone. If AI can do any thinking work, it can write, edit and even pick the stories. The only thing left is standing at the side of the pitch with a phone, and robots doing that are about three years behind, maybe 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab anything at the clubs, even part-time matchday work, because being physically there is the last bit to go. I'd move back in with my dad, who lives twenty minutes away, and save every penny of rent. I'd look at a sports coaching qualification too, since coaching kids is hands-on and people-heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is not long enough to land anything solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say when you asked to move in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say fine, as long as I do the washing up and come to watch his darts team. He's a practical man. My dad would tell me he always said I should have been a PE teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned coaching. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I've coached the under-tens at my old club on Sundays, so it's not out of nowhere. Whether anyone pays for it when everyone's job is shaky, I honestly don't know.

say: This is happening **too fast**, and government needs to slow or cushion it.
He'd share views from people who **know more** than him.
think: By 2028 his **reporter job** is gone, as AI can write, edit and pick stories.
Standing at the **pitch side** is the last bit, until robots around 2031.
do: Take any **matchday work** at the clubs, even part-time.
Move back in with his **dad** to stop paying rent.
Start a **sports coaching** qualification, building on Sunday coaching.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years isn't enough to land anything solid.
S2.quote: My dad would tell me he always said I should have been a PE teacher.
fieldNote: Uses the **3-year robot gap** to plan matchday and coaching work.
Family is a **real fallback**: his dad would take him in.
Coaching plan rests on **real experience** with the under-tens.

steps.text: Take part-time matchday work at the local clubs
Move back into his dad's house to save rent
Start a junior sports coaching qualification
Share calls online for government to cushion the change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives clubs, papers and governments time to plan, and they'd better use it. I'd probably say it on the radio commentary if anyone asked. Nothing heated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I could get out ahead of it. My reporting job still fades by 2031, but I'd have time to land a club media role or get coaching badges first. I wouldn't be grabbing at anything going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the first coaching badge and keep doing the Sunday under-tens. I'd apply for the club media officer roles and learn whatever AI tools the clubs use for their own content. I'd try to save a month's rent by dropping the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I believe in more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait for others to try things first. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the AI stuff, yes, I'd copy what other club media teams do. For the coaching badge, no, I'd start now, because there's no downside. It's cheap and I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the paper would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production editor, who builds the pages every night. He's fifty-five with a mortgage. My worry is less for me than for people like the production editor, because I can always move home.

say: Five years gives clubs, papers and governments **time to plan**.
He'd say it **calmly**, maybe on radio commentary.
think: His reporting job still **fades by 2031**, but there's time to move first.
He could land a **club role** or coaching badges without grabbing at anything.
do: Start the **first coaching badge** and keep Sunday coaching.
Apply for **club media** roles and learn their content tools.
Drop the **car** to save a month's rent.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan he believes in more.
S3.quote: My worry is less for me than for people like the production editor, because I can always move home.
fieldNote: Five years turns grabbing into **choosing**, which lowers his mood.
Starts **cheap moves** at once and waits on the costly ones.
His **dad's home** is a safety net he knows others lack.

steps.text: Take the first level coaching badge this year
Apply for club media officer roles at local clubs
Learn the AI content tools club media teams use
Give up the car to save a month's rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for sport to work out what it wants from humans, and fans will still want people. I'd say that on the radio and at five-a-side. It's a fairly hopeful thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because I'd be thirty-seven with a career that ended halfway. But ten years is long enough to become a properly qualified coach or get into teaching. My reporting job goes, but my life doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for three or four years and get better at video. I'd do coaching badges step by step and look at a part-time PE teaching course around year three. I'd try to save properly, a month's pay in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, in the background. More like a niggling injury than a broken leg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been seeing my girlfriend for a few months, and I'd be careful about moving in together until I knew where I'd land. I'd still want it eventually. I just wouldn't sign a lease I couldn't cover alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a teenager who wants to be a sports reporter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a teenager to learn to coach or film or present as well, not just write. Writing a match report is the first thing machines learned. Standing in front of people is harder to replace.

say: Ten years is enough for sport to decide what it wants from **humans**.
**Fans** will still want people, which is a hopeful thing to say.
think: He'd be **thirty-seven** with a career ended halfway.
Ten years is long enough to become a **qualified coach** or get into teaching.
do: Keep reporting for **three or four years** and improve at video.
Do coaching badges and a **part-time PE** teaching course around year three.
Save a **month's pay** in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** in the background, like a niggling injury rather than a break.
S4.quote: My reporting job goes, but my life doesn't.
fieldNote: Expects the **reporting role** to end even with ten years, so still anxious.
A slow pivot to **coaching and teaching** fits his steady style.
Cautious about a **shared lease** he couldn't cover alone.

steps.text: Keep reporting for three or four years while improving video skills
Enrol in a part-time PE teaching course around year three
Save a month's pay in the first year
Hold off signing a shared lease with his girlfriend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be scrambling with no money and no qualifications outside journalism. What would help is cheap or free coaching and teaching courses for people switching careers, with a bit of income while you train. Also, honestly, clubs being encouraged to hire local people for the matchday jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what fans want. I think a lot of supporters would rather read a reporter who was in the rain with them than a perfect machine summary. Whether owners pay for that is another question.

headlineQuote: A lot of supporters would rather read a reporter who was in the rain with them than a perfect machine summary.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old sports reporter** for a regional daily's website, living alone in a studio flat.
He uses AI **now and then** and moves once others have proven a tool works.
He's **uneasy** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** under AGI by 2028, when match reports go first.
His fallback runs through **club media**, coaching the under-tens and his dad's spare room.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no money and no qualifications outside journalism.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **coaching and teaching** courses with income while training.
Clubs hiring **local people** for matchday jobs.
